questions.text: A complaint of 30 words contains the word 'denied' 3 times. What is tf('denied', this document)?
options: Depends on the number of documents
questions.explanation: tf(t, d) = count(t, d) / total words in d = 3 / 30 = 0.10. Term frequency is always normalised by document length so that long and short documents are on a comparable scale.

questions.text: The word 'insurance' appears in 490,000 of 500,000 documents. What is its idf?
questions.explanation: idf(t) = log(N / df(t)) = log(500000 / 490000) = log(1.0204) ≈ 0.020. This very low idf means 'insurance' is nearly useless for distinguishing documents — it carries almost no information.

questions.text: Why do we use the logarithm in the idf formula?
options: To ensure idf values are always between 0 and 1
To compress the range of N/df(t) so that very rare terms do not overwhelm very common terms
Because the natural logarithm converts word counts to probabilities
To make idf values negative for very common words
questions.explanation: Without the log, N/df(t) can be enormous for rare terms, dominating TF-IDF. The log compresses the scale: log(1) = 0 (term in every doc), log(N) ≈ constant (term in only one doc). This gives a reasonable range and preserves relative ordering.

questions.text: You use unnest_tokens(word, complaint_notes) followed by anti_join(stop_words). What does anti_join do here?
options: Joins the word frequency table with a dictionary of important words
Keeps only words that DO NOT appear in the stop_words lexicon
Removes rows from stop_words that appear in the complaint notes
Adds a sentiment score to each word
questions.explanation: anti_join(words, stop_words, by = 'word') returns all rows from 'words' that do NOT match any word in the stop_words table. This efficiently removes common non-discriminating words like 'the', 'a', 'is'.

questions.text: A bigram tokenisation of 'not covered' produces one token ('not_covered') rather than two ('not', 'covered'), which is advantageous when negations matter.
questions.explanation: Unigrams lose negation: 'not covered' and 'covered' both contribute the token 'covered' equally. Bigram tokenisation keeps 'not_covered' as a single token, preserving the negation. This is especially useful for sentiment analysis and complaint classification.

questions.text: The document-term matrix is described as 'very sparse'. What does this mean?
options: Most documents are very short (fewer than 20 words)
Most cells contain very small (near-zero) TF-IDF values
Most cells contain zeros because most terms appear in only a small fraction of documents
The matrix has more rows than columns
questions.explanation: With thousands of unique terms and tens of thousands of documents, most (term, document) combinations have count = 0 because each document uses only a small fraction of the total vocabulary. In practice, 95-99% of DTM cells are zero. Sparse matrix formats (as used by topicmodels) exploit this structure to save memory.
